title: The shutter
question: How do you make a piece of plastic move that fast, the same way every time?
hook: Press the rocker. Click. For about three thousandths of a second a window in a plastic blade swings past the lens and the film gets its picture. No motor, no battery, no spring from a shop. One printed blade, and a trick you already do with your fingers.

sections.title: Your guess first
sections.body: Three hundred of these openings would fit into one second. And the whole shutter is one piece of printed plastic: a blade with a hole in it, sitting on a peg. Nothing you could buy in a shop, nothing wound up.
sections.q: When you press the rocker, what decides how fast the blade swings past the lens?
choices: Something else that does not care about your finger
sections.reveal: Something else. There is no spring to buy, and fingers are hopeless timers: by the model, a slow push with nothing to snap would let in about eleven times the light of a quick one. The camera uses a click. Your finger only loads it. Keep reading: you will build the proof yourself in two experiments.

sections.title: Fast, and the same every time
sections.body:
In daylight film needs only a sip of light. Too long and the picture comes out muddy; too long and anything moving smears. So the shutter has to open for a tiny moment, about 1/322 of a second, and do it the same way whether your finger is quick or lazy.

Fingers are hopeless timers. The fix is a snap. Press your finger against your thumb harder and harder: nothing moves. Then it slips and all the stored push goes at once. You can't snap slowly.

The blade does exactly this. Its own thin rim is the spring. A tooth on the rim sits in a notch; press the rocker and the tooth climbs the notch's slope, the rim bends, nothing moves yet. At about 2.3 newtons, the weight of a big apple, the tooth jumps out and the blade flies through its swing. Your finger loads the click. The click decides the speed.

figure.caption: One blade, one window, one peg.

timeline.what: Pictures take minutes. The shutter is a lens cap: off, count, on.
Eadweard Muybridge fires twelve cameras with tripwires and shows a galloping horse with all four feet off the ground.
Drop shutters: a plate with a hole falls or is pulled past the lens. Your blade is the same idea, swung.
Clockwork shutters with thin leaves that open like an eye, up to 1/250 s.

sections.label: Why this piece exists

sections.title: Freeze the horse, slow the blade

sims.intro: A horse at full gallop covers about 16 metres a second. Pick a shutter time and see what the film would get.
sims.after: Blur is speed × time. At 1/322 s the horse moves 5 cm and the legs stay crisp. At 1/28 s it moves 57 cm and the legs dissolve.

sims.intro: Press the rocker in slow motion, a hundred times slower, with a clock in real thousandths. Then take the click away.
sims.after: With the click, a slow finger only changes the wait before the snap; the swing takes the same 3 thousandths or so. Without it, a slow push leaves the window open eleven times as long.

sections.title: The blade and the rocker
sections.alt: A finger pressing the teal rocker on top of the camera
sections.caption: One quick press of the rocker.
sections.body:
Building the shutter takes a second: lay the front plate face down and drop the blade onto its peg, rocker over the edge. The rocker is a shallow V; press the raised side, and next time the other side is up.

The secret middle click: press only halfway and the window stops right over the lens. The shutter stays open while you count, for pictures in dim light. Stand the camera on something first.

sections.title: A shutter with no blade
sections.body: Most phones have no blade at all. The sensor is told to start collecting light, then read out, all electronically, so a phone can open for many seconds at night or for far less than a thousandth in sun. Here's a mind-bender: slow-motion video at 240 pictures a second takes one picture every 4.2 thousandths of a second. Your shutter's whole opening, 3.1 thousandths, fits in the gap.

sections.title: What the click saves
sections.summary: one sum, with the real numbers
lines: a slow push with no click: about 1/28 s
8 is 3 steps, 16 is 4 steps: 11.5 is about 3.5 steps
full sun, small dot, ISO 400, with the click: half a step over
with a slow push: 0.5 + 3.5 = 4 steps over: outside the film's 3
sections.body: The film forgives 3 steps too much (lesson 3). The click keeps you well inside; a lazy finger would not.

sections.title: Catch the window on film
needs: your camera, with no film inside
a phone that films slow motion
a pile of books to stand it on
steps: Stand the phone 10 to 15 cm from the camera's front, so the lens and the rocker are both in view. Light the front well.
Set the large dot. Start the slow motion.
Press the rocker flat in one quick press, then the other side. Stop filming.
Play it back frame by frame and count the frames where the window is over the lens.
Now press as slowly as you can until it clicks. Film it and count again.
sections.notice: Quick press or slow press, the window shows for about the same number of frames. The click, not your finger, sets the time.

items.q: What actually lets light reach the film in this camera?
choices: A gap that opens between two blades
A round window in one swinging blade
The lens moves out of the way
items.why: One teal blade with one window. At rest solid plastic covers the lens; a press swings the window across it once.

items.q: You press the rocker very slowly. What happens to the picture?
choices: Much brighter on the print: more light got in
Nothing different: the click lets go at the same push every time
Nothing at all: a slow press doesn't fire
items.why: Nothing moves until the push reaches the click, about 2.3 N. Then the tooth jumps out and the blade flies at about the same speed however slowly you pressed.

items.q: Without the click, a slow push gives about 1/28 s. Roughly how many steps more light than 1/322 s is that?
items.why: 322 ÷ 28 = 11.5 times the light. 8 is 3 steps and 16 is 4, so 11.5 is about 3.5 steps. Careful: 11.5 is the times, not the steps.

items.q: A horse runs at 16 m a second. How far does it move while this camera's shutter is open (1/322 s)?
items.why: 16 ÷ 322 = 0.05 m = 5 cm. A couple of percent of the horse: sharp enough to count its legs.

items.q: It's a dim room. How do you take a picture?
choices: Press it to the middle click, count, then press on down, with the camera on something steady
items.why: At the middle click the window stops over the lens, so it stays open while you count: a time picture. With ISO 400 and the small dot, lamps on: count 5.

sections.title: Try it on your roll
sections.lead: About a three-hundredth of a second. Find out what that freezes.
shots: A friend jumping, in full sun, small dot, about 2.5 m away. Press smoothly, don't stab.
Something crossing in front of you: a bike, a runner, a dog. Same light, same dot.
sections.look: The jump should hang in the air, sharp. The bike may smear a little sideways: at 20 km/h it moves about 17 mm while the shutter is open.

sections.body: One picture taken. Now the film has to move on exactly one picture, no more, no less.

units.what: 5 questions, then 2 pictures to take on your roll in your own time.

objectives: Describe how this shutter makes a picture: a blade with one window swings once past the lens.
Explain why a click gives the same speed whatever the finger does, and why a plain push would not.
Work out that a slow push (about 1/28 s) lets in about 11.5 times the light of a click (about 1/322 s), about 3.5 steps, and say why that spoils the picture.
Use speed × time to work out how far a moving thing travels while the shutter is open.
Take a time picture with the rocker's middle click.
materials: Per group of three: one built camera with no film in it, a phone that films slow motion, a stack of books, paper, pencil, calculator
For the drop-shutter demo: a rubber band, two rulers, a card with a hole, a torch
The page on a projector for the two sims and the film
teach.exit_ticket: In one sentence: what decides how fast the shutter moves, your finger or the click? Why? And one number: about how many times more light does a slow push let in? (About 11 or 12.)
teach.misconception: That a fast shutter needs a strong spring and a fast finger, and that the photographer's press decides the speed. In its place: the finger only loads a click; the click lets go at a fixed force, so the speed is the same whoever presses.

differentiation.support: Give the sum as a fill-in-the-blanks card (322 ÷ 28 = __). Use the gallop sim's readouts instead of calculating blur. Pair readers with confident talkers for the Try card's write-up.
differentiation.stretch: Design a way to time 3 thousandths of a second with school kit (a light sensor on a data logger, or a phone's light meter app recording). Or: using speed × time, find the slowest shutter that keeps a sprinter (about 10 m/s) under 1 cm of blur.
differentiation.access: Both sims work with the keyboard and describe every result in words. The Try card works without a phone: listen to the click and feel for the middle one.

teach.safety: No film in cameras used for slow motion. Nobody points a camera or phone at the sun. The rubber-band drop shutter is aimed at the desk, not at faces.

period.what: Show the question and 'Your guess first' on the board. Every student writes A, B or C. Count; do not correct yet.
The story and its timeline, quickly: lens caps to Muybridge. Drop a card with a hole past a torch beam: the drop shutter.
Groups do the Try card (catch the window on slow motion). Groups that finish early run the gallop sim.
Snap your fingers slowly: impossible. The blade sim in slow motion, with the click and without it.
The sum on the board, then the quiz in pairs. Then the middle click: each group holds the rocker there and sees the window stay open: a time picture.
Exit ticket. Return to the opening vote: who changed their mind, and why?

questions.q: Why did shutters only become a problem after 1839?
questions.a: At first pictures took minutes and a lens cap was fine. When plates got faster, hands were too slow.

questions.q: Why does a quick press and a slow press give the same picture?
questions.a: Nothing moves until the push reaches the click (about 2.3 N). Then it all lets go at once, so the blade always flies at about the same speed.

questions.q: A slow push lets in 11.5 times the light. Is that inside the film's window?
questions.a: 11.5 times is about 3.5 steps; with the half step full sun already gives, 4 steps over. The film forgives 3: outside.

questions.q: How far does a car at 30 m/s move while the shutter is open?
